421.title: The anthill
421.hook: a riddle of an anthill that smokes by night and blazes by day: the body (MN 23)
421.howItsDone: Theravada teachers sometimes use the anthill riddle to teach the hindrances and the aggregates, and in many Buddhist traditions the naga, a serpent, is an image of the awakened one.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the raft, and your line, put the raft down. Did you let go of one thing you were done with? Day four hundred twenty-one.

Late one night in a dark forest, a young monk named Kumara Kassapa is visited by a deity who lights up the whole grove, and gives him a riddle. There's an anthill, the deity says. It smokes by night and blazes by day. A brahmin said: wise one, take a tool and dig. Digging, the wise one found a bar. Then a bullfrog. Then a fork in a road. Then a strainer, a tortoise, a butcher's knife and block, a piece of meat. And at last, a naga, a serpent. And the brahmin said: leave the naga. Don't disturb it. Honor the naga. Go ask the Buddha what it means. Today: the anthill.
screen: `A RIDDLE IN THE DARK.` → `IT SMOKES BY NIGHT, BLAZES BY DAY.` → `DIG.`

segments.voice: MN 23, the Vammika. Kumara Kassapa does what he's told and takes the riddle to the Buddha, who opens it piece by piece. The anthill is this body: made of the four elements, born of mother and father, built up of rice and porridge, subject to wearing away and breaking apart. Smoking by night is lying awake thinking over what you did by day. Blazing by day is acting on those thoughts by day, in body and speech. The brahmin is the Buddha himself. The wise one is a disciple in training. The tool is noble wisdom. Digging is effort. Then, what the digging turns up. The bar is ignorance: lift it out. The bullfrog is angry despair. The fork in the road is doubt. The strainer is the five hindrances. The tortoise is the five aggregates, the pieces we take for a self. The knife and block are the five cords of sense pleasure. The piece of meat is delight and lust. Each one: lift it out, throw it away. And the naga, the serpent, is a monk whose taints are destroyed: leave it, honor it. What's striking is the order of things. You dig through layer after layer of obstacles, the plain, heavy stuff of a mind, and at the bottom you don't find a monster. You find something to honor. The commentary says Kumara Kassapa later reached awakening by working with this very riddle. It was given to a beginner, and it took him all the way.
screen: `THE ANTHILL IS THIS BODY.` · `NIGHT THINKING, DAY DOING.` · `BAR, FROG, FORK, STRAINER, TORTOISE.` · `AT THE BOTTOM, A NAGA TO HONOR.` · then, large: `DIG CAREFULLY.`

segments.voice: Sit, and feel the anthill: this body, sitting here, built of food and breath. Notice whether it's smoking: thoughts from last night, plans from today, still turning over. Then dig gently, one layer. Is there a fork in the road here, a doubt? A bullfrog, some irritation puffing itself up? Just name what you find, and lift it out on an out-breath. No need to reach the bottom today. The bell holds the time.
The anthill. A riddle about the body, dug through layer by layer with wisdom, until there's something at the bottom to honor.
Your line: dig carefully. Tonight, before you sleep, notice what's still smoking from the day, and name it once. Day four hundred twenty-one.

match.prompt: match each piece of the riddle to its meaning.

myth: at the bottom of the anthill is a monster to destroy
it's a naga, and the brahmin says to leave it and honor it.
the brahmin in the riddle stands for the Buddha
and the wise one is a disciple in training.
the tortoise stands for the five aggregates
the pieces we take for a self.

fork.setup: digging the anthill, you finally uncover a naga, a serpent. what does the brahmin say to do?
options: kill it
leave the naga; honor the naga
keep digging past it
fork.reveal: leave it and honor it. everything else is lifted out; the naga stands for one whose taints are destroyed.

original.note: Pali vammika: an anthill or termite mound, the name of MN 23.

trapdoor: what you thought: a strange fairy tale.
what it means: a riddle about the body: dig with wisdom, lift out each obstacle, and honor what's at the bottom.
what a scholar hears: the commentary says Kumāra Kassapa reached arahantship by working with this sutta; nāga, a serpent or elephant, is a common Pali image for an awakened one.

422.title: Relay chariots
422.hook: seven chariots in relay, each for one stage of the road
422.howItsDone: In Theravada teaching the seven purifications from this discourse became the frame of later meditation manuals, most famously Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga, where a practitioner's progress is described stage by stage, each purity resting on the one before.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the anthill, and your line, dig carefully. Did you turn over one piece of your own anthill, slowly, without hacking at it? Day four hundred twenty-two.

Two monks have heard of each other for years and never met. One is Sariputta, the Buddha's chief disciple for wisdom. The other is Punna, son of Mantani, praised by everyone who knows him. Sariputta wants to meet him. So he follows Punna into a grove called the Blind Men's Wood, sits down under a tree a little way off, and when the afternoon is ending, walks over and starts asking questions. Punna has no idea who he's talking to. Today: relay chariots.
screen: `TWO MONKS WHO NEVER MET.` → `A GROVE, A TREE, AN AFTERNOON.` → `PUNNA DOESN'T KNOW WHO'S ASKING.`

segments.voice: This is the twenty-fourth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings. Sariputta asks: why do you live the holy life? For pure virtue? No. For a pure mind? No. For pure view? No. He goes down a list of seven purities, and Punna says no to every one. Then what for? For final release without clinging, Punna says. Then is final release the same as pure virtue? No. Is it something apart from all seven? Also no. So Punna gives a picture. King Pasenadi lives in Savatthi and has urgent business in Saketa, a long way off. So he sets out seven chariots in relay along the road. He rides the first to the second, climbs down, rides the second to the third, and so on, until the seventh brings him to the palace gate in Saketa. Now someone at the gate asks: did you come here from Savatthi in this chariot? If the king says yes, that's not quite true. The honest answer names the whole relay. Each chariot only had to reach the next one. That's how the seven purities work, Punna says. Pure virtue is for the sake of a pure mind. A pure mind is for the sake of pure view. And so on down the road, until the last purity carries you to release. None of them is the goal. None of them can be skipped. Then the two men learn each other's names, and each praises the other. A good day for both of them. Here's what it says to an ordinary Tuesday: you don't have to ride the whole road today. You only have to reach the next chariot.
screen: `WHY DO YOU LIVE THE HOLY LIFE?` · `SEVEN CHARIOTS FROM SAVATTHI TO SAKETA` · `EACH ONE ONLY REACHES THE NEXT` · `NONE IS THE GOAL; NONE IS SKIPPED` · then, large: `ONE STAGE AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one stage today. Think of something long you're in the middle of: a recovery, a degree, a hard year, a habit you're rebuilding. Don't picture the finish. Picture only the next chariot, the one small stretch that's actually in front of you this week. Then let the picture go and sit with the breath, one breath as one stage, then the next. When the mind runs ahead to the palace gate, bring it back to this chariot. The bell holds the time.
Relay chariots. Seven purities, each one there to carry you to the next, until the last brings you to release. Today's word.
Your line: one stage at a time. Today, when the whole road feels too long, name only the next chariot, and ride that one. Day four hundred twenty-two.

myth: Punna says the goal of the holy life is pure virtue
he says no to all seven purities: the goal is final release without clinging.
the king could honestly say one chariot brought him
the honest answer names the whole relay: each chariot only reached the next.
the seven purities can't be skipped
each one is for the sake of the next, all the way to the last.

fork.setup: you're King Pasenadi, arriving at the palace gate in Saketa. someone asks: did this chariot bring you all the way from Savatthi? what's the honest answer?
options: yes, this one.
no: seven chariots, each to the next.
no chariot brought me; I walked.
fork.reveal: Punna's point: the last chariot only covered the last stretch. the whole relay brought the king, the way seven purities carry someone to release.

original.note: Pali ratha: chariot. the discourse is called the Rathavinita Sutta, the relay of chariots.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a king's travel plans.
what it means: each stage of practice exists to carry you to the next one, and none of them is the goal by itself.
what a scholar hears: MN 24's seven purifications later became a guiding frame for Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga, the Path of Purification, usually dated to the fifth century.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 24, Rathavinita Sutta (the relay chariots)

423.title: The bait
423.hook: the deer-feeder's crops, laid out to catch four herds
423.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the Nivapa Sutta's four herds to describe the middle way between indulgence and harsh denial; monastics and lay meditators practice restraint of the senses and deep concentration as the 'lair' Mara can't reach.

segments.voice: Yesterday: relay chariots, and your line, one stage at a time. Did you ride only the next chariot, and let the rest of the road wait? Day four hundred twenty-three.
screen: `RELAY CHARIOTS — ONE STAGE AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: A phone game is free. The first level is easy, the colors are bright, and there's a little gift waiting every morning if you open it. Nobody built that by accident. Somebody sat in a room and planned how you'd be caught, gently, so you'd never feel the net. Twenty-five centuries ago the Buddha described the same room, only with a field and a herd of deer. Today: the bait.
screen: `FREE, BRIGHT, A GIFT EVERY MORNING.` → `SOMEBODY PLANNED IT.` → `A FIELD, AND A HERD OF DEER.`

segments.voice: This is the twenty-fifth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings. A deer-feeder plants a crop, not out of kindness, but so deer will come, eat carelessly, and be easy to catch. Four herds come. The first herd walks straight into the crop, eats without care, grows heedless, and is caught. The second herd sees this and swears off the crop entirely. They go deep into the forest and live on wild grass. But in the last month of the hot season the grass and water run out. They grow thin and weak, wander back to the crop, eat wildly, and are caught too. The third herd is smarter. They make a lair close by and eat carefully, never losing their heads. But the deer-feeder notices them, puts up a great fence around the field, finds where they sleep, and catches them as well. The fourth herd makes its lair where the deer-feeder can't go. They eat without losing their heads, and slip away. The feeder and his men can't find them. Then the Buddha explains. The crop is the five cords of sense pleasure: sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touches that pull at us. The deer-feeder is Mara, the tempter. The herds are four kinds of seekers: those who dive in, those who run to harsh denial and break, those who stay close and get trapped by opinions, and those who go where Mara can't follow, into deep stillness. Notice the second herd. Running away wasn't enough. Starving wasn't freedom. The way out is neither the crop nor the desert. It's eating without being caught.
screen: `A CROP PLANTED TO CATCH DEER` · `FOUR HERDS: DIVE IN, RUN, HOVER, ESCAPE` · `THE CROP IS THE FIVE CORDS OF PLEASURE` · `RUNNING AWAY WASN'T ENOUGH` · then, large: `THE BAIT IS SET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one bait set for you. Sit, and think of the last time today you reached for something without deciding to: the phone, the fridge, the feed, the cart. Don't judge it. Just see the field it grew in: who planted it, and how bright it looked. Then come back to the breath, which nobody is selling you. Rest there. If the pull comes again during the sit, watch it rise like a deer lifting its head, and stay where you are. The bell holds the time.
The bait. The deer-feeder's crop: pleasures laid out on purpose, so we'll eat carelessly and be caught. Today's word.
Your line: the bait is set. Today, once, when something bright pulls at you, say the line quietly, and then choose: eat carefully, or walk on. Day four hundred twenty-three.

fork.reveal: the second herd starved and came back; the third was fenced in. only the fourth herd, eating without infatuation where the feeder couldn't go, slipped away.

original.note: Pali nivapa: bait, fodder laid out. the discourse is the Nivapa Sutta.

trapdoor: what you thought: pleasure is the enemy.
what it means: the trap is eating carelessly; fleeing into harsh denial failed too.
what a scholar hears: the fourth herd's lair stands for the meditative absorptions (jhana), described in MN 25 as places where Mara loses sight of the practitioner.

424.title: The noble search
424.hook: the ignoble search chases what ages; the noble search seeks the unaging
424.howItsDone: Many Buddhists hear MN 26 as the Buddha's own account of his going forth and awakening, and teachers use its two searches to invite reflection on aging, sickness and death, often in the daily recollection that one is subject to them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bait, and your line, the bait is set. Did you catch one bright thing pulling at you, and choose how to meet it? Day four hundred twenty-four.

Open the search history on almost any phone. Shoes. Flights. A better job. Is this mole normal. Houses we can't afford. Whether a certain person is still single. It's a strange, honest diary: a list of what we're hunting for. The Buddha once sorted every search a person can make into just two kinds. And he started by admitting which kind he had been making himself. Today: the noble search.
screen: `A SEARCH HISTORY IS A DIARY.` → `WHAT ARE WE HUNTING FOR?` → `ONLY TWO KINDS OF SEARCH.`

segments.voice: This is the twenty-sixth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the Ariyapariyesana Sutta. Ariya means noble. Pariyesana means search. The Buddha says there are two searches. In the ignoble one, a person who is themselves subject to aging, sickness and death goes looking for happiness in things that are also subject to aging, sickness and death. He lists them plainly: family and servants, goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, elephants, horses, gold and silver. None of these is wicked. The point is only that they age too. You're chasing something that is running out at the same speed you are. In the noble search, a person who sees that they are subject to aging and death looks for what does not age and does not die: the unborn, the deathless, the supreme security from bondage. Buddhists call it nibbana, nirvana in Sanskrit. Then the discourse does something unusual. The Buddha tells his own story, in his own voice. Before awakening, he says, he too was making the ignoble search. Then, while still young, black-haired, in the first stage of life, he shaved his head and went forth, though his mother and father wept. He studied with two great teachers, mastered what they taught, and left both, because it wasn't yet the end of the search. He walked until he reached a pleasant grove at Uruvela with a clear river, sat down, and there found what he was looking for. So the noble search isn't throwing away the shoes or the house. It's noticing what you're asking them to do. They can't stop you aging. Something else might be worth a search of its own.
screen: `ARIYA: NOBLE · PARIYESANA: SEARCH` · `CHASING WHAT AGES, AS YOU AGE` · `SEEKING THE UNAGING, THE DEATHLESS` · `THE BUDDHA'S OWN SEARCH, TOLD BY HIM` · then, large: `THE NOBLE SEARCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: seek one lasting thing. Sit, and think of the last three things you searched for, on a screen or in your head. Hold each one lightly and ask: will this age? Almost always, yes. That's fine. Then ask a different question: what in me was looking, underneath? Rest? Safety? To be loved? Let that deeper wish sit with you, without solving it. Breathe with it. That wish is where a noble search begins. The bell holds the time.
The noble search. Ariyapariyesana: a being who ages, seeking what does not age. Today's word.
Your line: the noble search. Today, the next time you type into a search bar, pause for one breath and ask what you're really looking for. Day four hundred twenty-four.

they aren't wicked; they simply age and pass, like the one who seeks them.
in MN 26 the Buddha tells his own story
he says he too made the ignoble search, then went forth while young, though his parents wept.
he stayed with his first two teachers to the end
he mastered what they taught and left both, because it wasn't yet the end of the search.

fork.setup: you've mastered everything a famous teacher knows. he offers to share leadership of his community with you. what do you do?
options: accept: you've reached the top.
leave: this isn't the end of the search.

fork.reveal: in MN 26 the young seeker leaves both of his teachers, because what they taught didn't lead all the way to the deathless.

original.note: Pali pariyesana: search, seeking. ariyapariyesana: the noble search.

trapdoor: what you thought: a noble search means giving up everything you own.
what it means: it means seeing that what ages can't save you from aging, and looking for what doesn't.
what a scholar hears: MN 26 holds one of the oldest first-person accounts of the Buddha's going forth, his two teachers (Alara Kalama and Uddaka Ramaputta) and his awakening.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 26, Ariyapariyesana Sutta (the noble search)

425.title: The smaller footprint
425.hook: a good tracker doesn't conclude from a small footprint; the gradual training
425.howItsDone: Theravada teachers often present MN 27 as a model of the gradual training, from hearing the teaching and keeping precepts to meditation and liberation, and use the tracker's patience to caution students against mistaking early meditative experiences for the goal.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the noble search, a being who ages looking for what doesn't. Did you pause before one search and ask what you were really looking for? Day four hundred twenty-five.

A wanderer named Pilotika comes out of the forest full of admiration for the Buddha. A brahmin asks him why he's so sure the Buddha is the real thing. Pilotika says: I'm like an elephant tracker who sees a huge footprint and knows, that's a great bull elephant. I've seen four footprints of this man, and I'm sure. The brahmin carries the story to the Buddha. And the Buddha, of all people, says: not so fast. Today: the smaller footprint.
screen: `PILOTIKA IS SURE.` → `FOUR FOOTPRINTS, ONE GREAT ELEPHANT.` → `THE BUDDHA: NOT SO FAST.`

segments.voice: This is the twenty-seventh discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the shorter discourse on the simile of the elephant's footprint. The Buddha finishes Pilotika's picture properly. A skilled tracker enters an elephant forest and sees a big footprint, long and broad. He doesn't conclude. There are female dwarf elephants with big feet. Then he sees a big footprint, and high marks where the bark is scraped. Still he doesn't conclude. Tall female elephants could make those. Then he sees high tusk marks and broken branches. Still not. Only when he sees the bull elephant itself, under a tree or in the open, does he say: this is the great one. Then the Buddha lays out the gradual training. Someone hears the teaching, gains trust, and goes forth. They keep the precepts. They guard the senses, eat in moderation, stay mindful in everything they do, and find a quiet place to sit. The hindrances fall away. They enter the first absorption, then the second, the third, the fourth. Each of these, the Buddha says, is a footprint. But a noble disciple doesn't conclude yet. Then come deep knowledges, and still not. Only at the end, when the mind is freed and they know it's freed, do they say: the teacher is truly awakened, and the teaching is well proclaimed. It's a strange thing for a teacher to say about his own followers' praise. Slow down. A good feeling in meditation is a footprint, not the elephant. A good first week at anything is a footprint. Keep tracking.
screen: `PILOTIKA'S PRAISE, AND A CORRECTION` · `A BIG PRINT COULD BE A SMALLER ELEPHANT` · `THE GRADUAL TRAINING, STEP BY STEP` · `ONLY THE ELEPHANT ITSELF SETTLES IT` · then, large: `NOT YET THE ELEPHANT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: don't conclude too soon. Sit, and let the breath come and go. Within a few breaths, the mind will offer a verdict: this is going well, or this isn't working, or I'm bad at this. Notice the verdict. Call it a footprint. Then keep sitting, and see what comes next. If another verdict arrives, call that a footprint too. You're tracking, not deciding. The bell holds the time.
The smaller footprint. A big print that might belong to a smaller animal: a sign worth following, not yet a reason to conclude. Today's word.
Your line: not yet the elephant. Today, when you catch yourself deciding about a person or a situation from one sign, say the line, and wait for more tracks. Day four hundred twenty-five.

pairs: could be a female dwarf elephant

he said the simile wasn't complete yet, and finished it properly.
in MN 27 even the four absorptions are only footprints
a noble disciple doesn't conclude from them; only liberation settles it.
a skilled tracker concludes from the biggest print
big prints can belong to smaller elephants; he waits to see the bull itself.

fork.setup: you're a tracker. you find a long, broad footprint and high scrape marks on the trees. what do you conclude?
options: a great bull elephant, for sure.
nothing yet: tall females can leave these too.
it's a trap; go home.
fork.reveal: the Buddha's tracker keeps going past every sign until he sees the bull elephant itself, in a clearing or under a tree.

original.note: Pali hatthipada: elephant's footprint. hatthi (elephant) + pada (foot, footprint).

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about being careful in the forest.
what it means: every good sign along the path is a footprint, worth following, not yet the goal.

what a scholar hears: MN 27 is a classic statement of the gradual training (anupubba sikkha), the same sequence that appears in many discourses, from going forth through the jhanas to the destruction of the taints.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 27, Culahatthipadopama Sutta (the shorter simile of the elephant's footprint)

426.title: The heartwood
426.hook: a man seeking heartwood who settles for twigs, bark or sapwood
426.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the heartwood simile to remind monastics and lay practitioners that reputation, good conduct, concentration and insight are stages of the path, and that liberation of mind is its goal.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the smaller footprint, and your line, not yet the elephant. Did you wait for more tracks before deciding about someone? Day four hundred twenty-six.

Anyone who has built a fire with green branches knows the problem. It smokes, it hisses, it goes out. The good wood is inside: the dense, dark center of an old tree that burns slow and lasts. Carpenters want it too. It doesn't rot, it doesn't warp. You can't get to it without cutting through everything else first: the leaves, the bark, the pale sapwood. And it's tempting to stop halfway. Today: the heartwood.
screen: `GREEN BRANCHES SMOKE AND GO OUT.` → `THE GOOD WOOD IS AT THE CENTER.` → `TEMPTING TO STOP HALFWAY.`

segments.voice: This is the twenty-ninth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings. It was given, the text says, not long after Devadatta, the Buddha's cousin, had split away from the community. The Buddha describes a man who needs heartwood. He goes into the forest, finds a great tree, and walks past the heartwood, past the sapwood, past the inner bark and the outer bark, and cuts off twigs and leaves. He carries them home thinking he's got heartwood. A man with good eyes would say: he doesn't know what heartwood is. His work won't get done. Then the Buddha maps the tree. Someone goes forth out of faith, and gains gifts, honor and fame. Pleased with that, they look down on others. That's the twigs and leaves. Someone else doesn't stop there and becomes truly virtuous, but stops pleased with their virtue. That's the outer bark. Another goes on to deep concentration, and stops there. Inner bark. Another reaches knowledge and vision, and stops. Sapwood. And then the discourse says the goal plainly. This holy life is not for gifts and fame, not for virtue alone, not for concentration alone, not for knowledge and vision alone. It's for the unshakable freedom of mind. That is the heartwood. Notice: none of the outer layers is bad. Virtue is good. Concentration is good. They're part of the same tree. The mistake is only in stopping, pleased with yourself, and calling bark heartwood. It's an easy mistake in any serious work. The applause, the good habits, the skills: real, and still not the center.
screen: `TWIGS AND LEAVES: GIFTS AND FAME` · `BARK: VIRTUE, THEN CONCENTRATION` · `SAPWOOD: KNOWLEDGE AND VISION` · `HEARTWOOD: UNSHAKABLE FREEDOM OF MIND` · then, large: `TAKE THE HEARTWOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go for the heartwood. Pick one thing you care about: your work, your practice, a relationship. Sit, and ask what its twigs and leaves are: the praise, the likes, the look of it. Then what its bark is: the good habits around it. Then ask quietly what's at the center, the part that would still matter if nobody saw. Rest your attention there for the rest of the sit, as if your hand were on the grain of the wood. The bell holds the time.
The heartwood. Sara in Pali: the dense core of the tree, past the leaves, the bark and the sapwood. The unshakable freedom the path is for. Today's word.
Your line: take the heartwood. Today, when praise or a small success comes, enjoy it, and then ask what's still at the center. Day four hundred twenty-six.

they're real layers of the same tree; the mistake is stopping there, pleased, and calling bark heartwood.
the text places this talk soon after Devadatta split away
MN 29 opens not long after Devadatta left the community.
the man in the story carries home sapwood
the first man walks past everything else and carries home twigs and leaves, thinking it's heartwood.

fork.setup: you went forth, and people now bring you gifts and praise your name. what does the Buddha's simile call that?
options: the heartwood.
the twigs and leaves.
the sapwood.
fork.reveal: gifts, honor and fame are the twigs and leaves: the outermost part of the tree, the furthest from the heartwood.

original.note: Pali sara: heartwood, the core or essence. the discourse is the Mahasaropama Sutta, the greater simile of the heartwood.

trapdoor: what you thought: be a good person and you've arrived.
what it means: goodness, focus and insight are layers of the tree; the path is for unshakable freedom at its center.
what a scholar hears: Pali sara means both heartwood and essence, so the simile's title carries both senses at once.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 29, Mahasaropama Sutta (the greater simile of the heartwood)

427.title: Milk and water
427.hook: Anuruddha and his friends live blended like milk and water
427.howItsDone: Buddhist monasteries still share chores in much the way MN 31 describes, and the phrase 'like milk and water' is often used by Buddhist teachers to describe the ideal of a harmonious community, lay or monastic.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the heartwood, and your line, take the heartwood. When praise came, did you ask what was still at the center? Today, the end of a week, and three friends in a forest. Day four hundred twenty-seven.

Every shared kitchen has the same quiet war. Who finishes the milk and doesn't buy more. Who leaves the pan soaking for three days. Who takes the trash out, every single time, and has started keeping score. Three monks once lived together in a sal-tree wood called Gosinga. When the Buddha came to visit, he asked how they were getting along. Their answer has been quoted ever since. Today: milk and water.
screen: `THE QUIET WAR IN A SHARED KITCHEN.` → `THREE MONKS IN A SAL-TREE WOOD.` → `HOW ARE YOU GETTING ALONG?`

segments.voice: This is the thirty-first discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings. The three are Anuruddha, Nandiya and Kimbila. When the Buddha arrives, the park keeper tries to turn him away, not knowing who he is, so as not to disturb the monks. Anuruddha hears, and comes running. Then the Buddha asks: are you living in harmony? And Anuruddha says yes: we live without quarreling, blending like milk and water, looking at each other with kind eyes. How? the Buddha asks. Anuruddha says: I think, how fortunate I am to live with companions like these. I treat them with kindness in deed, word and thought, openly and in private. And I think, why don't I set aside what I want, and do what they want? So I do. We are different in body, he says, but one in mind. Then he describes the kitchen. Whoever comes back first from the alms round sets out the seats and the water. Whoever comes back last eats what's left or throws it out, and puts everything away. Whoever sees the water jar empty fills it. If it's too heavy, he waves a hand for help, and the two of them carry it together, without breaking the silence. And every fifth night they sit up together, talking about the teaching. Milk and water mix so completely you can't pour them apart. Not because either disappears, but because neither is keeping score. Look back at this week: an anthill dug carefully, relay chariots, the bait, the noble search, a footprint, the heartwood. Today the whole path turns up in a water jar carried by two.
screen: `THE PARK KEEPER TRIES TO TURN HIM AWAY` · `KINDNESS IN DEED, WORD AND THOUGHT` · `WHOEVER SEES THE JAR EMPTY FILLS IT` · `THIS WEEK: FROM AN ANTHILL TO A JAR` · then, large: `MILK AND WATER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be easy with one person. Think of someone you share space with: a home, an office, a group chat. Picture them clearly. Then try Anuruddha's thought, just to see how it feels: how fortunate I am to live with this person. It may feel strange. Let it. Then picture one small thing you could do for them today without being asked and without mentioning it: the jar, the dishes, the trash. Breathe with that picture. The bell holds the time.
Milk and water. Lives blended so well they pour as one: kind in deed, word and thought, each setting aside what they want for the others. Today's word.
Your line: milk and water. Today, fill one empty jar for someone you live or work with, quietly, and don't keep score. Day four hundred twenty-seven.

fork.setup: you're one of the three monks. you come back last from the alms round. there's leftover food and the seats are still out. what do you do?
options: leave it for whoever was first; they set it up.
eat what's left or throw it out, and put everything away.
call a meeting about fairness.
fork.reveal: in Anuruddha's description, whoever comes back last eats what's left or throws it out, and puts the seats and water away. nobody needs to be asked.

original.note: Pali samagga: in concord, united. the Buddha's first question to the three is whether they live in concord.

trapdoor: what you thought: harmony means never disagreeing.
what it means: it means kindness in deed, word and thought, and quietly doing your share without keeping score.
what a scholar hears: Anuruddha's formula (kindness of body, speech and mind, openly and in private) reappears in MN 48 among the six qualities that make for harmony.
